newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: South Asia seen on path to be poorest region.
newsitem.headline: South Asia seen on path to be poorest region.

text.p: South Asia is fast emerging as the world's poorest, most illiterate and malnourished region, a U.N.-aided human development study report by a Pakistani centre said on Wednesday.
"Nearly 40 percent of the world's poor live in South Asia," said the report by the Human Development Centre (HDC).

"South Asia is fast emerging as the poorest, the most illiterate, the most malnourished, the least gender-sensitive -- indeed the most deprived region in the world. Yet it continues to make more investment in arms than in education and health of its people," it said.

HDC president and former Pakistani finance minister Mehbub-ul-Haq told Reuters: "South Asia started ahead of Africa in 1960, its literacy rate was higher than Africa, but today South Asia's literacy rate is lower than in Africa.
"South Asia is also poorer than Africa, which many people do not realise," he said.
Haq said present per capita income in South Asia was US$309, compared to $555 in the Sub-Sahara region, the poorest part of Africa.
The HDC says its study was assisted by the U.N. Development Programme's field offices in the region.

Haq said the report was intended to draw attention to South Asia after its eclipse by troubles in Africa, and to urge developed countries to invest in a region with a population of about 1.2 billion people compared to Africa's 500 million.
"The world has forgotten us. They are so worried about Africa because of Somalia, Rwanda, Burundi and Nigeria," Haq said.
"So most of the world's attention has been going on to Africa and most of world's aid. Most of concessional resources have been going to Africa."

Haq said he had no objection to the focus being on Africa, but the world should not forget to invest political and economic capital in South Asia..."because if this region disintegrates, you will forget Rwanda and Burundi".
The report urged governments in the region to start preparing for the 21st century by investing in education, health and other social sectors.
"We are saying to national planners, wake up, you are not ready to enter the 21st century and don't pretend you will be industrialised tigers of tomorrow," Haq said.
The report said South Asian countries needed to invest an average of $8.5 billion each year on education, health, nutrition, credit to poor people and social services.
Haq said the region, which includes arch-foes India and Pakistan, could obtain the required funds by cutting military spending and reducing tensions in the area.
